newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Analysts see no Yugo reform in election year.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see no Yugo reform in election year.

text.p: Yugoslav economists believe that any radical reform of the Serbian economy is unlikely in the election year and say the government's only policy is to squeeze scarce funds out of banks and enterprises.

"The measures give government direct control of the enterprises. This is counter-productive and is bringing us back to central planning," said Stojan Stamenkovic, leading economist of the Belgrade-based Institute for Economics Sciences.
"Unfortunately our economy will be based on discretionary political decisions instead of plans," he told Reuters.
The cash-strapped economy, which endured four years of war-related sanctions, is still barred from fresh funds abroad, the only means of salvation for the now idling production.

Economists have been saying for months Serbia needed radical market reforms but at the same time they believe President Slobodan Milosevic would avoid taking any steps that could jeopardise his already precarious political standing. But not doing anything may cost Milosevic's Socialists dear. The elections are due by the end of the year.

"No government is prepared to pay the high cost of radical reforms. They will inevitably lead to social unrest and socialists will lose their voters," said Dana Popovic, an analyst in the private Centre for Economic Studies CES Mecon.

The recent Serbian cabinet reshuffle, under which a privatisation portfolio was created, has so far not produced any reform of the way in which the economy is run. Meanwhile, economic data available paints a gloomy picture.
Public revenues have dropped drastically and reached a two-years record low in January.
Starved for fresh cash, with wages and pensions running late, the government must find money to cover its growing public spending deficit and stay intact and ready for elections later this year.

The government moved towards centralising scarce funds by revoking licences to insolvent commercial banks that remain outside of its control. But it left intact those enjoying government protection and whose managers are close to the ruling Socialists, analysts say.
"This is aimed at creating giant banks for easier state control and discretionary distribution of available funds," Stamenkovic said.
Economists estimate that the current government lacks $110 million per month to pay wages, salaries and cover its costs.

Industrial sources say that in order to boost revenues, the government is preparing selective privatisations, such as the currently negotiated sale of the postal company. The government aims to earn $700-800 million from the sell-offs, but the rules of the process are unclear and no details are available.

The government is working on a privatisation law, due to be presented to parliament by the end of March. Leaks indicate the law will not be transparent and aims only at beefing up the government's coffers, analysts said.
A source close to the government said any serious reforms could not start without new funds.

"Empty state coffers have forced the government to centralise available funds for easier and more efficient distribution. It is a necessity and not a desire," the source said. -- Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
